{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and, in the text field, the passage of about 250 words that came immediately BEFORE the current text in its story.","text":"By the time Mara returned from her mother’s house, the rain had started again. It followed her up the steps of the apartment building and tapped at the windows while she unpacked the last of the boxes she had brought back from the coast.

Most held ordinary things: two chipped bowls, a stack of old photographs, a wool coat that still smelled faintly of cedar. Her mother had insisted that Mara take them, though neither of them had been able to say why. They had spent the afternoon sorting in silence, pausing only when they came across something that demanded a story.

There had been no stories about Bellweather. Whenever Mara asked about the village, her mother found a reason to change the subject. Her grandfather, she said, had been a difficult man. He had left before Mara was old enough to remember him, and it was better not to go looking for meaning in what people left behind.

Mara had accepted that explanation for years. Lately, though, she had begun to wonder whether silence was simply another kind of inheritance. At the bottom of one box, beneath a bundle of yellowed postcards, she had found a photograph of her mother as a girl, standing beside a stone wall. A small dark shape was visible near her hand—perhaps a key, perhaps only a shadow.

She had meant to ask about it before leaving. But her mother was already at the door, one hand on the knob, her face turned away.

“Take care of yourself,” she had said.

Now Mara set the photograph on her desk and went to rinse the mug she had been holding since she got home. Outside, rain blurred the streetlights. The building’s old pipes clicked in the walls, and somewhere in the hall, a door opened and shut."}
